results.one_line: Bosnia's state AML law (13/2024) requires bookkeepers, accountants and real estate brokers to keep a written risk assessment, internal acts and client files, and inspectors in both entities are checking them now (FATF grey-listed BiH in June 2026); no local tool generates these documents, but the market is a few thousand price-sensitive micro firms with a mostly one-off need.
results.buyers: An estimated 2,500-5,000 obliged small entities (unverified): mostly bookkeeping firms and sole bookkeepers, plus 135 FBiH real estate agencies (Ministry of Trade register via prostor.ba), RS/Brcko agencies, auditors and dealers. FBiH section M had 4,535 legal entities and 4,068 natural-person businesses in Dec 2022 (FZS), but that section includes many non-obliged professions.
results.price: Today buyers pay 150-170 KM + VAT for a one-day Paragraf AML seminar (2025 fee) and unknown amounts to consultants. A plausible price is a 150-300 KM one-off kit plus about 15-30 KM a month for the client register and yearly update (unverified), against fines of 20,000-80,000 KM for a missing risk analysis.
results.top_competitor: Copied templates and consultants. The closest product is A-count, a Croatian AML workflow for accounting offices with no BiH version or public price. Paragraf Lex seminars come next. FUZIP gives free questionnaires and guides, but no tool that generates the documents.
results.killer: No outright killer. The biggest risk is a small, resentful, price-sensitive market whose need is mostly a one-off document set that Paragraf, consultants or a free FUZIP/FOO template could cheaply cover.

results.one_line: Mexican private-security firms must report every staff, uniform, vehicle, arms and branch change to the DGSP Registro Nacional by day 10 of each month (LFSP art. 13). DGSP fined firms MXN 113k-170k for this in 2026 and no dedicated tool exists, but the firm count, the filing channel and willingness to pay are unproven.
results.buyers: About 8,000+ private-security firms (AMESP estimate cited in a Sept 2026 Chamber of Deputies bill, gaceta.diputados.gob.mx). No official count: the DGSP open-data list was last updated in 2018. State samples: Jalisco 289, Chihuahua 269, Puebla about 250. AMESP has 250 members.
results.price: Plausible MXN 1,500-5,000 per month per firm, tiered by headcount (unverified). Today firms pay in-house gestores or gestorías (fees not published). Fine exposure is MXN 113,140-169,710 per sanction (DOF 2026), and a guard costs more than MXN 10,000 a month.
results.top_competitor: None found for the DGSP Registro. The real alternative is in-house gestores and gestorías, with generic guard-operations apps (C-Guard Pro, GuardsPro/Guardso, Guardhouse) that ignore Mexican filings.
results.killer: None found. Biggest risk: the DGSP submission channel and format are unknown (an in-house DGSP portal would shrink the value). Also the overdue Ley General de Seguridad Privada (mandated in 2021, not issued) could reset the register, and the market is fragmented and price-sensitive across 32 state regimes.

results.one_line: Paraguayan real-estate firms owe a heavy, enforced AML routine under SEPRELAD Res 201/2020 (KYC, risk matrix, manual, quarterly negative reports, annual internal evaluation and external audit), and only about a third file their audits. The free SIRO portal only receives filings. The market is about 1,450 small firms (plus about 850 car dealers) with low price anchors and warning-only enforcement, so it is a niche business best sold through registered auditors.
results.buyers: 1,451 real-estate firms paid the SEPRELAD annual canon in 2025, plus 845 car dealers, 108 jewellers, 23 pawn shops and 6 cash-in-transit firms (SEPRELAD public stats portal, seprelad.gov.py/siro/estadisticaExterna). GAFILAT MER 2022 counted 1,658 registered real-estate subjects. Real-estate firms filed 7,474 negative reports but only 492 external audits in 2025.
results.price: About US$25-60/month SaaS or US$300-600/year compliance pack (my estimate), ideally bundled with the mandatory external audit. Today firms pay SEPRELAD's annual canon of about Gs 329k (about US$45) and a registered external auditor (fee unverified). Filing in SIRO is free.
results.top_competitor: SEPRELAD's free SIRO portal and free risk-matrix/capture forms (Res 240/241 of 2020). Partial private overlap: Compliance Paraguay PEP database. No local SaaS for the full workflow found.
results.killer: None found that kills it outright. Biggest risk is the small market (about 1,450 firms) plus weak monetary enforcement: 1,238 warnings to real-estate firms in 2024, and only 1 fine in all sectors in 2025. SEPRELAD could also extend its free SIRO/forms into KYC and risk modules.

results.one_line: Licensed Israeli gemachim face a real 2019 law, a 2026 sector AML order and a draft AML circular (written policy, yearly board review, AML officer, risk assessment, training, 31 March Excel report). But only about 170 bodies have applied, 7 are licensed, the state supplies the reporting template and portal for free, and the rules phase in 18 months or more after final publication, so this suits a niche compliance service rather than SaaS.
results.buyers: About 170 licence applicants (ICE, Dec 2025; Calcalist, Aug 2025; about 140 in Feb 2023 per Walla). About 20 were 'mature' and 7 were licensed by Sept 2026 (Funder snippet). Gemachim under NIS 1m are exempt.
results.price: No published prices were found. Gemachim are donation-funded volunteer bodies and price-sensitive. An estimated NIS 300-1,000/month for an outsourced AML officer plus software is plausible for mid-size funds (unverified). Large funds (NIS 1bn+) can pay more.
results.top_competitor: The free Capital Market Authority Excel template and portal (reportsportal.cma.gov.il) for the yearly AML report. No gemach-specific software found. Generic lending systems (CAV Systems) and Nedarim Plus are possible rivals (unverified).
results.killer: None found. The main weaknesses are a tiny market (about 170 applicants, 7 licensed) and slow phase-in (the circular takes effect 18 months after final publication, and licensees get 2 years to prepare). The yearly filing itself is free via a state template, and the community is closed and hard to reach.

results.one_line: Edinburgh's levy is live and its first return (due 30 Oct 2026) asks for monthly figures for each premises: revenue split by booking date and the 5-night cap. That is a real but narrow gap for a tool that turns OTA exports into the return, held back by a small Scottish market, a 2% retention that keeps prices low, PMS vendors adding levy reports, and pressure for simpler flat-rate levies.
results.buyers: About 2,500-3,500 small liable providers in Edinburgh (an estimate): 3,209 short-term let licences at 31 Dec 2025 (Scottish Government STL statistics) plus about 200 guest houses and B&Bs (2019 Ryden/GVA count via Lichfields). Glasgow (Jan 2027), Aberdeen (from Apr 2027), Stirling and West Dunbartonshire (2027) could add roughly 2,000-4,000 more (estimate). No count of providers registered on visitorlevy.scot is published.
results.price: About £5-10 per property per month, or £20-40 per quarterly return (estimate). Today buyers pay nothing for filing (visitorlevy.scot is free) or get the levy features bundled in a PMS (freeonlinebooking, Hop, Bookster, freetobook); no standalone priced tool was found. That price is set against a 2% retention (about £30 a year for a typical unit) and Edinburgh penalties: first late return about £108-£398 (residential) or 1% of rateable value, and 10% for late payment.
results.top_competitor: The free state platform visitorlevy.scot (filing, payment and a calculator) together with PMS levy reports, of which freeonlinebooking's emailable levy reports are the most complete.
results.killer: None decisive. The biggest risk is that the market stays small and cheap: PMS vendors bundle levy reporting, and councils move to flat per-night rates (allowed by the 2026 Amendment Act and pushed by the STA), which would turn the sum into nights x rate.

results.one_line: CBK's new rules for non-deposit-taking credit providers (reported as LN 191 of 2026) give every credit-only lender until about 29 March 2027 to apply for a licence or registration, and the application needs about six written policies plus fit-and-proper paperwork. CBK says most of its 800+ pending applications are stuck waiting for documents, so a lawyer-reviewed application pack plus a compliance calendar could sell. The buyer pool is small and the rush is a one-off.
results.buyers: Roughly a few hundred to about 1,000 firms; this is my estimate (unverified). Official figures: CBK has received 800+ DCP applications since 2022, and 252 were licensed by July 2026 (CBK press release, 14 Jul 2026), rising to 281 by September 2026 (TechTrendsKE), which leaves roughly 500 pending, withdrawn or rejected. CBK says the pending ones are "largely awaiting requisite documentation". On top of that come newly covered offline lenders: logbook, asset finance, BNPL, P2P and moneylenders. I found no official count for them; one commercial site says about 250 are on a CBK register (unverified). The 281 already-licensed DCPs do not need to reapply, so they are buyers only for ongoing compliance tooling.
results.price: About KES 60k-150k (USD 450-1,150) for a one-off application pack, plus KES 5k-15k a month for a complaints register and compliance calendar. Today buyers pay CBK KES 100k to apply and KES 250k a year (registration) or KES 500k a year (licence), with a KES 1m late-fee penalty. Breaches can cost up to KES 2m plus KES 10k a day. ODPC data-protection fines on lenders have run from KES 250k to 5m. Law firms do licensing work, but I found no published prices (unverified).
results.top_competitor: Kenyan law firms selling done-for-you licensing (Bowmans, Cliffe Dekker Hofmeyr, CM Advocates, Oraro), together with CBK's free licensing and BSA returns portals. Loan-management vendors such as SuperLMS, Lendsqr and Craft Silicon cover regulator reporting but not the application. I found no dedicated NDTCP compliance product.
results.killer: None decisive. The main risks are a short one-off window (to about 29 March 2027) and a small pool that may shrink, because the fee jump from KES 20k to 250k-500k a year may push micro lenders out. The 2025 draft also excludes hire purchase and credit that is incidental to a sale. Selling drafted policies without an advocate may conflict with the Advocates Act (unverified).

results.one_line: Firearm dealers and armed security firms in South Africa must keep detailed registers that SAPS and PSIRA inspect often, and no local software does the job; but the market is a few thousand small firms, the rules lean toward paper books, and the stock data is very sensitive, so the opportunity is niche.
results.buyers: About 300 licensed dealer companies (old SAAADA submission, pmg.org.za/files/1/firearmsbill_SAAADA.htm). 3,340 security businesses held firearm licences, out of 8,345 institutions licensed by the CFR (PSIRA audit, PMG NW2280, 2017). PSIRA lists 16,704 registered security companies (PMG NW2477, June 2026). Ranges and gunsmiths are not counted. Estimate: about 4,000 to 8,000 obliged entities, with roughly 3,000 to 4,500 armed security firms as the core segment.
results.price: No published South African price for firearm register or armoury software was found. Today buyers pay for paper register books, armourer staff time and PSIRA registration agents (about R2,990 per job). International guarding SaaS costs EUR 4 to 9 per officer per month. A plausible price is R350 to R900 per site per month, plus R3,000 to R10,000 for an inspection-readiness audit (unverified estimate).
results.top_competitor: None local. The nearest options are paper DFO-stamped register books, US FFL point-of-sale systems (Rapid Gun Systems, AIM POS) and foreign armoury systems (NextGen IoT, FN SAM). Guard-management SaaS sold in South Africa (Tech Guarding, GuardsPro) could add an armoury module.
results.killer: No outright killer. The biggest risk is a small, paper-bound market: Reg 22 describes ink-written, numbered-page registers, and buyers are wary of putting firearm stock data in the cloud. A court-ordered SAPS dealer link (Reg 38 and the 2019 SAAADA order) could absorb the dealer returns, but SAPS has failed to deliver it since 2022.

results.one_line: The Czech wine evidence-book and declaration duty is real, with fines of up to 5M Kč, but at least four Czech tools (Sklepmistr, Vitipad, VineOS, eVin) already cover it for 2,500-3,800 Kč a year, and the market has only about 1,342 levy-paying wineries.
results.buyers: 1,342 levy-paying wineries in 2025: 1,061 small (under 20,000 l), 237 medium and 44 large (Vinařský fond fact sheet 2026). About 2,236 registered producers (MZe, around 2021). About 13,700 growers, mostly hobby-sized.
results.price: Incumbents charge VineOS Pro 2,490 Kč a year (with a free tier), Vitipad 3,800 Kč a year flat, and Vinservis eVin 1,200 Kč a month hosted. Agrowin Sklepmistr does not publish prices. A typical small winery pays only about 2,700 Kč a year in Wine Fund levy. A newcomer could charge at most about 2,000-4,000 Kč a year.
results.top_competitor: Agrowin Sklepmistr / Vinařský sešit and Vitipad, both taught in the state-subsidised Valtice wine academy course; VineOS also has a free tier.
results.killer: The earlier checks said there was no Czech vendor. That is wrong: four or more cheap local products already generate the decree 88/2017 evidence books and the ÚKZÚZ / Wine Fund declarations, and they share a tiny market of about 1,300 paying wineries.

results.one_line: Res. UIF 43/2024 gives licensed Argentine brokers a full AML programme (client risk files, monthly SROMasivo reports, a biennial self-assessment and external review) that no broker software covers, but thin enforcement and two-year cycles make this a modest tool, best sold white-label through the broker colegios.
results.buyers: No official count of brokers registered with the UIF exists. More than 40,000 licensed professionals nationwide (HCDN bill 6505-D-2024); COFECI says 35,000+; FIRA estimates 70,000+ agencies including unlicensed ones (iProfesional, Feb 2025). Obliged firms (those handling sales, or leases of 300 SMVM or more) are estimated at 10,000-25,000 (unverified). Only a few thousand are above the 875 SMVM external-reviewer threshold (unverified).
results.price: Unverified estimates: ARS 15,000-40,000 a month (about USD 10-30) as a compliance add-on, or ARS 150,000-400,000 per self-assessment cycle. Today brokers pay USD 80-300 a month for Tokko CRM and ARS 15,000-80,000 for InmoPC. Law-firm fees for a manual and risk matrix are unpublished. Fines run 15-2,500 módulos (ARS 0.8M-135M) per infraction.
results.top_competitor: The UIF's free SRO+/SROMasivo template handles only registration and filing of the monthly and annual reports. Beyond that, the FACPCE ITAER free matrix (written for accountants) and law firms such as ST Abogados. No broker-specific SaaS was found, and the Tokko, Xintel and InmoSuite CRMs have no AML module.
results.killer: None found. The biggest risk is weak enforcement and low willingness to pay: in 2024 the UIF imposed 25 fines across all sectors, the main deliverables recur only every two years (next due Apr/Aug 2028), and a colegio could build a free member tool as the notaries' colegio did. Licence deregulation could also weaken the colegio sales channel.
